index.note: Teaching order is NOT alphabetical. It follows the research-based sequence (high-frequency letters, continuous sounds first, visually confusable pairs kept apart) with two deliberate overrides: L moved to first because it starts {child}'s name, and A and T pulled forward so real word-building starts by week four instead of week ten.
index.sourceOrder: m s r t n p o c a d / g f b k i l h w / e v j u y z x q

b.seed: Lego: a bridge you've driven over. Bible: the friends who lowered their friend through the roof.

c.seed: Play-Doh: mix two colors, name the new one. Bible: the six days.

d.seed: Lego: a doghouse. Bible: David and the giant — courage, not violence.

e.seed: Crack a real egg. Bible: the empty tomb, told gently.

f.seed: Lego: a fishing boat. Bible: the disciples who fished.

g.seed: Plant one seed in a cup. Bible: the boy who gave his lunch.

h.seed: Lego: house on rock vs house on sand — then pour water on both.

i.seed: Freeze small toys in ice and excavate them.

j.seed: Bible: water into wine at the wedding — the jars are the hook.

k.seed: Fly a kite at a windy park. Bible: the good Samaritan.

n.seed: Build a nest from yard materials. Bible: Samuel hearing God at night.

o.seed: Aquarium trip tie-in. O is a circle — shape week.

p.seed: Lego: repeating color patterns. Bible: how to talk to God.

q.seed: Paper quilt squares — pattern math. Bible: Esther.

r.seed: Prism or water glass rainbow. Bible: Noah — God keeps promises.

t.seed: T unlocks mat, sat, at. Count to ten with truck loads.

u.seed: Positional words — under, over, beside. Real umbrella weather.

v.seed: Baking soda volcano — and some mountains are volcanoes. Bible: Jericho.

w.seed: Sink or float in a bowl. Bible: Jesus calms the storm.

x.seed: Treasure map with an X. X is rare — keep it short and playful.

y.seed: Yarn letter shapes glued on card. Bible: saying yes to God — Mary.

z.seed: Zoo trip. Zero is a real math idea — none of something.

l.subject: alphabet
l.whyThisOrder: Not a research-order letter — L is first because it starts {child}'s name. Name letters are the highest-motivation entry point for a 4-year-old, and recognizing {their} own name is a pre-reading milestone on its own.

sound.cue: Tongue tip up behind your top teeth, and hummmm: llllll. You can hold it as long as you have breath — that's what makes it easy to blend later.
sound.sayThis: The letter is named 'el'. The sound it makes is /l/. Say the sound more than the name.
sound.commonConfusion: Lowercase l and capital I look nearly identical in most fonts. Always show l inside a word (log, lamp) rather than alone.

formation.capital: Big line straight DOWN, then a little line ACROSS at the bottom. It looks like a chair turned sideways.
formation.lowercase: One tall line straight down. That's the whole letter — the easiest one in the alphabet.
formation.prewritingStroke: Vertical line + horizontal line. If {child} can't yet draw a straight vertical line on demand, spend the whole letter block on that and skip the paper.
practiceLadder: Sky-write it with a finger, big
Trace it in a tray of flour or salt
Trace a marker version you drew
Write it {themself} on a blank line

materials: Lego or Duplo bricks — needs about 20, including 1 yellow and some white or grey
A real leaf from the yard
Optional: shallow tray with flour or salt

blocks.title: Find your letter
blocks.parentScript: Write {CHILD} in big capitals across a page. Point at the L. "This one is L. It's the very first letter of your name. It says /l/."
steps: Have {them} point to the L {themself}.
Write {CHILD} again but leave the first letter blank. Ask {them} what's missing.
Let {them} fill it in any way at all — a scribble counts.

blocks.title: Making the L
blocks.parentScript: Say the sound, not the name, every time you point at it. "Down… and across. L says /l/."
steps: Sky-write a giant L with your whole arm. {child} copies.
Trace in the flour tray if you have one.
Draw three big dotted L's to trace over.
One L on {their} own. Praise the try, not the tidiness.

blocks.title: Build a lighthouse
blocks.parentScript: If there's a real lighthouse near you, pull up a photo of it first if that helps {them} picture it — or make it this weekend's trip.
steps: Stack a tall tower of white and grey bricks — count each one out loud as it goes on.
Put ONE yellow brick on the very top. That's the light.
Turn off the room light and shine the flashlight on it.
Then build the letter L flat on the floor: 5 bricks going down, 3 bricks going across the bottom.
blocks.extension: Ask {them} why a boat would want to see a light in the dark. Let {them} answer badly — the question is the point.

blocks.title: Leaf prints
blocks.parentScript: This one is fine-motor work disguised as art. Rolling and pressing builds the hand strength writing needs.
steps: Roll a long snake, then bend it into an L.
Flatten a ball into a pancake.
Press the real leaf into it hard, then peel it off — the veins stay behind.
"Leaf starts with /l/. Lllleaf."

blocks.title: Listening for /l/
blocks.parentScript: Say each pair out loud and stretch the first sound. {child} votes yes or no.
steps: "Llllion — does that start like {child}?" (yes)
"Bear — does that start like {child}?" (no)
Walk one lap of the house and find one real thing that starts with /l/ — lamp, lid, light.

blocks.title: God made the light
steps: Sit in a dark room with the flashlight off. "At the very beginning there was nothing to see. It was all dark."
Click the flashlight on. "Then God said, Let there be light — and there was light."
Let {them} click it on and off a few times and say it with you.
Point back at the Lego lighthouse: "God made light, and we get to make light too."

blocks.title: Leaping
steps: Put 5 paper L's on the floor as stepping stones.
Leap from L to L — say /l/ on every landing.
Then leap like a lion and roar. Lion starts with L too.

blocks.title: One question
steps: "What's something that makes light?"
Whatever the answer, say the /l/ sound one last time and stop. End while {child} still wants more.

bible.story: On the very first day of making the world, God spoke and light came.
bible.memoryPhrase: God said, Let there be light.
bible.note: Four-year-olds hold about five words. Don't extend the phrase.

math.how: Count each brick out loud as it goes onto the lighthouse tower. Touching one object per number word is the actual skill — reciting numbers fast is not.

media.label: L in action
media.channelHint: Alphablocks — shows letters making sounds inside words

books.title: Chicka Chicka Boom Boom
books.author: Bill Martin Jr.
books.why: The alphabet book that actually holds a 4-year-old. Read it any letter week.

books.title: Leaf Man
books.author: Lois Ehlert
books.why: Pairs directly with the leaf print.

adaptations.ifTooHard: Drop the paper writing entirely. Flour-tray tracing and the Lego L are enough — letter formation on paper often isn't ready at four.
adaptations.ifTooEasy: Write {CHILD} and let {them} copy the whole name. Or add a second yellow brick and ask how many lights now.
adaptations.ifWiggly: Go straight to the leaping block, then come back. Movement first is not a failure mode, it's a strategy.

m.subject: alphabet
m.whyThisOrder: First letter in the research-based sequence. /m/ is the easiest sound in English to produce and hold, the letter is visually distinct from everything else, and it starts a word {child} already says all the time.

sound.cue: Lips closed, hum: mmmmm. Like tasting something good. It buzzes — put {their} fingers on your lips, then on {their} own.
sound.sayThis: The letter is named 'em'. The sound is /m/. Lead with the sound.
sound.commonConfusion: m and w are the same shape flipped. Don't teach w anywhere near this week.

formation.capital: Down, slant down, slant up, down. Like two mountains side by side.
formation.lowercase: Down, then a hump, then another hump. "Down, over the hill, over the hill again."
formation.prewritingStroke: Vertical line plus diagonal. Diagonals are harder than verticals at four — expect wobble.
practiceLadder: Trace in flour or shaving cream

materials: Lego or Duplo — about 25 bricks, with several white ones
A basket or small container and a doll or stuffed animal

blocks.title: The buzzing sound
blocks.parentScript: "Put your fingers on my lips. Mmmmmmm. Feel that? Now you do it."
steps: Hum /m/ together with fingers on lips.
"Mmmmom. Mmmmilk. What else starts that way?"
Write a big M and a small m on paper and leave them visible all session.

blocks.title: Two mountains
blocks.parentScript: Use the mountain language every single time — it's the hook that makes the shape memorable.
steps: Draw a huge M and say "down, up the mountain, down the valley, up the mountain, down."
{child} sky-writes it.
Trace three dotted M's.
Try one on {their} own. Two humps is the goal; evenness is not.

blocks.title: Build a snowy mountain
blocks.parentScript: If you can see a mountain from a window, look at it first. Otherwise pull up a photo of a snowy one.
steps: Build a wide base row, then a shorter row on top, then shorter again — a staircase going up both sides.
Put white bricks on the top three rows. That's the snow.
Count how many rows tall it got.
Then build a capital M flat on the floor: two towers with a V of bricks between them.
blocks.extension: "Why is the snow only on top?" Let {them} guess. Then: it's colder way up high. That's {their} first science fact about a real mountain.

blocks.title: Six muffins
steps: Roll six balls and press one into each cup of the muffin tin.
Count them: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 — touch each one as you say it.
Take two out. How many are left? Count again.
Roll one long snake and bend it into an M.

blocks.title: Mmm or not?
steps: Say a word, stretched: "Mmmmap." Thumbs up if it starts with /m/.
Mix in some that don't: dog, moon, cup, mud, fish, milk.
Then go find something in the kitchen that starts with /m/.

blocks.title: Baby Moses in the basket
blocks.parentScript: Keep the danger vague. The point is not Pharaoh — the point is that God took care of a baby, and takes care of {them}.
steps: Put the doll in the basket. "There was a baby named Moses. His mom loved him so much and wanted him safe."
Float or slide the basket along the blanket like a river.
"A princess found him and kept him safe. God was taking care of Moses the whole time."
"God takes care of you too." Let {them} carry the basket around.

blocks.title: March
steps: March around the room saying /m/ /m/ /m/ on each step.
Freeze when you say STOP.
Then climb the couch like a mountain.

blocks.title: One question
steps: "Who takes care of you?"
Whatever {child} names — you, family, Jesus, the dog — take it. Then done.

bible.story: Baby Moses is hidden in a basket on the river, and God keeps him safe.
bible.note: Alternative if you'd rather: manna in the desert (Exodus 16), big idea 'God gives me what I need.' Also an M.

math.how: The muffins. Six out, take two away, count what's left. Subtraction at four means physically removing objects — never symbols.

books.title: If You Give a Moose a Muffin
books.author: Laura Numeroff
books.why: Two M words in the title and {child} will ask for it again.

books.title: Goodnight Moon
books.author: Margaret Wise Brown
books.why: Moon. And it's already in the bedtime rotation.

adaptations.ifTooHard: Skip the lowercase m entirely — two humps is a lot of motor control. Capital M only.
adaptations.ifTooEasy: {child} now knows M and L. Write 'am' and 'ma' and stretch them out loud. Blending two sounds is the next real milestone.
adaptations.ifWiggly: March first, mountain second, everything else optional.

s.subject: alphabet
s.whyThisOrder: Second in the research sequence. Another continuous sound to hold and stretch, and capital S and lowercase s are the same shape at two sizes — one of the only letters where that's true, so it's double value for one lesson.

sound.cue: Teeth together, air hissing out: sssssss. Like a snake, like a leaky tire.
sound.sayThis: The letter is named 'ess' — which already contains its own sound, so this one is easy to confuse in a helpful direction.
sound.commonConfusion: S gets written backwards constantly at this age. Reversals are developmentally normal until about 7 — correct gently once, then let it go.

formation.capital: Start at the top, curve back toward the door, then swing around the other way. Two curves that disagree.
formation.lowercase: Exactly the same, just smaller. Say so — it's a gift.
formation.prewritingStroke: The S-curve is the hardest stroke in this batch. Do it in Play-Doh and in the air many times before any pencil touches paper.
practiceLadder: Trace a giant S you drew, with a finger

materials: Lego or Duplo — a good handful in at least 4 colors
Cotton balls and a paper plate or cardboard
A small toy sheep or any stuffed animal

blocks.title: Snake sound
steps: Hiss together. Long as you can, then longer.
"Sssssun. Sssssock. Sssssnake."
Draw a big S and trace it with a finger while hissing — the sound lasts as long as the finger moves. That link matters more than it looks.

blocks.title: Sort, then snake
blocks.parentScript: Sorting by one attribute is a real pre-math skill and it looks like cleanup. Do the sorting first while {their} attention is fresh.
steps: Dump the bricks out. Sort them into color piles — one pile per color.
Count each pile. Which pile is biggest? That's comparing quantities.
Now build a snake: one long wiggly line of bricks, offset left and right so it bends.
Make it hiss across the floor.
blocks.extension: Sort the same bricks a second way — by size instead of color. Understanding that the same objects can be grouped differently is a genuine cognitive jump.

blocks.title: The two curves
steps: Roll a Play-Doh snake, then curl it into an S. Do it three times.
Sky-write the S big, slow, narrating the two curves.
Trace three dotted S's on paper.
One on {their} own. If it's backwards, say "good S!" and draw one next to it facing the right way. That's the whole correction.

blocks.title: The lost sheep
blocks.parentScript: This is the most interactive Bible block in the set. Play it like hide and seek, because that's what it is.
steps: Glue or press cotton balls onto the plate to make a sheep. Add a face.
"A shepherd had 100 sheep. One got lost. Do you know what he did? He went and looked until he found it."
Hide the toy sheep while {child} covers {their} eyes. Let {them} search.
When {child} finds it — "That's how happy Jesus is about YOU."
Say it together: "The Lord is my shepherd."

blocks.title: Sound hunt
steps: Walk the house and find three things starting with /s/ — sock, soap, spoon, stairs, sink.
Line them up and hiss each one.
If {child} already knows M and A: write 'Sam' and stretch it — ssss-aaaa-mmm. Blending may or may not happen yet. Either is fine.

blocks.title: Slither and stomp
steps: Slither across the floor on your bellies like snakes.
Stomp like something heavy. Both start with /s/.
Spin — then stop. Stop starts with S too.

blocks.title: One question
steps: "Can you find one more thing that starts with sssss?"
One is enough. End on a win.

bible.story: A shepherd leaves the whole flock to find one sheep that wandered off, and carries it home happy.
bible.bigIdea: Jesus looks for me and is glad when He finds me.
bible.note: Five words, and it's the single most useful verse fragment a kid can carry into adulthood.

math.skill: Sorting and classifying by attribute; comparing 'more' and 'fewer'
math.how: The color piles. Sorting precedes counting developmentally — it's how a child learns that things belong to groups at all.

books.why: Rhyme plus a wall of S sounds.

books.title: Sheep in a Jeep
books.author: Nancy Shaw

s.wrapUp: Can you find one more thing that starts with sssss?

adaptations.ifTooHard: Skip written S entirely. Play-Doh S and the sound hunt carry the whole lesson.
adaptations.ifTooEasy: {child} has M, S, and A after this batch. Write 'Sam', 'am', 'as' on cards and stretch-read them together.
adaptations.ifWiggly: Lead with the lost sheep hide-and-seek. It's movement and Bible at once.

a.subject: alphabet
a.whyThisOrder: The first vowel, and the one that unlocks words. With M, S and A, {child} can build 'am', 'as', 'Sam', 'mas' — the moment letters stop being decorations and start being a code. Teach the SHORT sound first; the long name 'ay' comes much later.

sound.cue: Mouth open, doctor-says-ahh but shorter: /a/ /a/ apple. Tap your chin on each one.
sound.sayThis: This is the one place the letter's NAME actively misleads. The letter is named 'ay' but it says /a/. Say the sound almost exclusively this week.
sound.commonConfusion: Don't mention the long A sound at all yet. One sound per letter until the code is solid.

formation.capital: Slant down this way, slant down that way, then a belt across the middle. Like a tent with a bar.
formation.lowercase: Around, and down. One circle and one line — the 'a' in most books has a curl on top, but the one to write is round.
formation.prewritingStroke: Circle plus vertical line. {child} can probably already do both — this is the first letter that puts two known strokes together.

materials: Lego or Duplo — about 20, with brown/dark, green, and several red 1x1s
Play-Doh, red and brown or green
A plastic knife or craft stick

blocks.title: The apple sound
steps: Hold up the real apple. "/a/ /a/ apple." Tap your chin each time.
{child} copies. Do it five times — it's short and choppy, not stretchy like M and S, and that difference is worth noticing.
Cut the apple in half crosswise so the seeds make a star. Let {them} see it before anyone eats it.

blocks.title: Tent with a belt
steps: Draw a big capital A: "slant, slant, belt."
Sky-write it three times.
Then lowercase a: "around, and down." Make the circle first, every time.
Trace dotted versions, then one freehand.

blocks.title: Apple tree
steps: Build a brown trunk — a tall stack of dark bricks.
Put a wide green plate or a flat spread of green bricks on top for leaves.
Stick red 1x1 bricks on as apples. Count them on.
Pick three apples off. How many are left? Count again.
Then build the capital A: two slanted stacks leaning toward each other with one brick across the middle.
blocks.extension: Ask where apples come from before the store. Trees, then seeds. Show {them} the seeds in the real apple you cut. That's a life-cycle conversation and it costs nothing.

blocks.title: Apples in half
steps: Roll three red balls. Add a brown stem to each.
Cut one in half with the plastic knife. "Now there are two HALVES. Two halves make one apple."
Put them back together. Take them apart again. Do it as many times as {child} wants.
Then make an ant: three small balls in a row, six tiny legs.

blocks.title: Adam names the animals
blocks.parentScript: This is the Bible story most likely to make a four-year-old feel like a participant. Let {them} take {their} time.
steps: Line up every stuffed animal in the house in a row.
"When God made the world, He made every single animal. Then He brought them all to the first man — his name was Adam — and let Adam give them their names."
"You get to be Adam. What should we call this one?"
Let {them} name every one. Write the names down, badly spelled, and keep the list.
"God made every animal. And He let people help take care of them."

blocks.title: The code cracks open
blocks.parentScript: This is the big one. If {child} blends even one word, that's the milestone — mark it in the log.
steps: Write 'am' in big letters. Point at each letter: "/a/… /m/… what's that word?"
Stretch it together slowly: aaaammmm. Then faster. Then: am.
Try 'as'. Then 'Sam' with three sounds.
If it doesn't click, say the word yourself cheerfully and move on. It clicks on its own schedule.

blocks.title: Ant crawl
steps: Crawl like ants carrying something heavy on your backs.
Ants can lift things way bigger than they are — let {them} try carrying a couch cushion.
Then be an alligator: arms out, snap, /a/ /a/ /a/.

blocks.title: One question
steps: "If you found a brand new animal nobody has ever seen, what would you name it?"
Write down whatever {child} says. Keep it. These are the notes you'll want in ten years.

bible.story: God brings every animal He made to Adam, and Adam gives each one its name.
bible.bigIdea: God made every animal, and He lets us help take care of them.
bible.note: Alternative if you'd rather: Noah's Ark (Genesis 6–9). Also an A, and also full of animals.

math.skill: Counting to 10, taking away, and first exposure to halves
math.how: Apples on the tree for counting and subtraction. Cutting the Play-Doh apple in half is {their} first fraction — physical, reversible, and named out loud.

adaptations.ifTooHard: Skip the blending block. Apples, ants, and naming animals is a full lesson on its own. Blending will come back around.
adaptations.ifTooEasy: Add 'mat', 'sat', 'at' — that needs T, but you can teach it on the spot in two minutes if {child} is hungry for it.
adaptations.ifWiggly: Animal naming first. It's sitting-still work that doesn't feel like it.
